title: Masks grown from wafers: electroformed nickel imprint stamps
idea: Po: the mask is the product. Pattern one perfect array-layer wafer once (EUV or e-beam), electroform nickel replicas of its etched topography, and use the Ni shims (thousands per master, like CD stampers) as nanoimprint templates for the periodic capacitor and bitline layers on production wafers.
why: Litho capex and EUV dependence (fact 4): replaces 2-3 EUV array exposures with NIL at ~1/5-1/10 the tool cost; templates become cheap consumables; ~15-25% wafer-cost cut if imprint defectivity is controlled.

title: Anodized aluminum pores as self-drawn capacitor molds
idea: Po: the metal draws its own circuit. Deposit thick Al, pre-dent it with a coarse DUV hexagonal guide grid, and anodize: self-ordered alumina pores form at 25-40 nm pitch with aspect ratios >150:1 in minutes; ALD TiN/high-k/TiN into the pores makes the capacitors with no high-AR plasma etch and no capacitor-hole EUV.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1) plus etch/litho capex: AR >115 reached chemically for ~1.5-2x Cs; deletes the costliest etch step and a SAQP/EUV hole layer.

title: Random cell placement mapped after fabrication by on-die address table
idea: Po: lithography happens after the chip is finished. Form cells by mask-free stochastic self-assembly (e.g., nanowire forests at random positions under a coarse word/bit grid), then at wafer sort electrically discover which crossings form working cells and burn a per-die logical-to-physical map into an on-die translation table, an FTL for geometry.
why: Overlay and litho cost (fact 4): eliminates tight-overlay array layers; trades ~10-20% array overprovision plus a small map SRAM for removing 3-5 critical masks.

title: Cleanroom-free fab: sealed wafer mini-environments in plain warehouse
idea: Po: the fab has no cleanroom. Keep every wafer in nitrogen-purged sealed pods and tool-integrated ISO-1 mini-environments docking through gasketed ports, so the building is an ordinary ISO-8 warehouse into which modular tool pods are trucked and plugged.
why: Fab capital and time (fact 4): cleanroom shell, makeup air and subfab are ~25-35% of construction cost and 1-2 years of schedule; ~20-30% lower fab $ and faster time to output.

title: Single grayscale exposure carves the entire 3D DRAM staircase
idea: Po: one exposure makes every layer. A multi-tone grayscale mask and a linear-contrast resist print a ramp of resist heights in one shot, and a proportional-selectivity etch transfers it into all 26-100 tier landing steps at once instead of dozens of trim-etch cycles.
why: 3D DRAM manufacturability (fact 2) and litho count: staircase from tens of trim-etch loops to ~1-3 litho+etch, ~5x cheaper, unlocking high tier counts.

title: Periphery micro-tiles fall into place by fluidic self-assembly
idea: Po: the transistors find their own seats. Make sense-amp/decoder micro-tiles on a cheap logic process, dice them into shape-keyed blocks, and flow them over array wafers with matching etched recesses where shape and capillary forces seat them; one RDL then wires them in.
why: Periphery ~49% of die (fact 7): array wafers carry only cells, roughly doubling bits per DRAM-fab wafer while periphery comes from cheaper nodes.

title: Grow capacitor pillars upward by area-selective deposition
idea: Po: no etching, only growing. Pattern only tiny seed pads, then use area-selective deposition (inhibitor-blocked dielectric, nucleating metal) to grow TiN or Ru pillars straight up ~1 um, followed by conformal high-k and top plate: the capacitor is built additively, not dug.
why: High-AR etch capex and capacitor wall (fact 1): removes the 60-75:1 mold etch, the slowest and costliest module step; height no longer limited by etch bowing.

title: Catalyst nanodots burrow into silicon to drill capacitor holes
idea: Po: the hole digs itself. Place Pt or Ag nanodots by imprint or self-assembly and run metal-assisted chemical etching in HF/H2O2: each dot sinks straight down, giving AR >100:1 holes in a wet bench; strip catalyst and line with high-k for trench-type storage capacitors.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1) and etch capex: wet bench ~1/20 the cost of a high-AR plasma etcher; AR >100 without bowing for Cs >8 fF.

title: Maskless interference lithography for perfectly periodic array layers
idea: Po: the pattern needs no mask. Because the cell array is a perfect lattice, expose array layers with multi-beam 193 nm interference that writes line/space or hexagonal hole lattices over a whole field with huge depth of focus, using a conventional scanner only to block out periphery.
why: Litho capex and EUV dependence (fact 4): interference exposure heads cost ~1/10 of a scanner and need no reticle; with pitch splitting they replace EUV for array layers.

title: Inspection-free fab using on-die sensors and boot-time self-repair
idea: Po: the fab never looks at its wafers. Remove most inline defect inspection and CD metrology; embed ring oscillators, capacitor-leak monitors and array test structures in every die that report process health at sort, and raise defect tolerance with 2x spare rows/columns plus boot-time soft remapping.
why: Capital intensity: inspection/metrology ~10-15% of tool capex plus cycle time; trades ~2% die area for ~10% lower capex and faster cycles.

title: Module micro-fabs: one plant per process module, wafers travel
idea: Po: a fab is spread across a country. Split the DRAM flow into module plants (transistor FEOL, capacitor module, BEOL/TSV) each sized to its bottleneck tool and linked by sealed-pod wafer logistics, so capacity grows one $1-3B module plant at a time instead of a $15B integrated fab.
why: Capital lumpiness and time (fact 4): smaller capex steps, faster ramps, U.S. siting of individual modules, higher tool utilization.

title: One scaffold printed, then every later layer self-aligns
idea: Po: lithography stops at the first layer. Print a single sacrificial lattice scaffold, then form word lines, bit lines, contacts and capacitor landing pads by successive spacer, selective-etch and selective-deposition steps referenced to it, so no later layer needs overlay.
why: Overlay budget and mask count (fact 4): critical masks from ~5-7 EUV to ~1-2; removes overlay-limited yield loss at F~12 nm.

title: Multibeam e-beam direct write replaces masks for irregular layers
idea: Po: masks don't exist. Use a ~250k-beam electron writer (today's mask-writer technology) directly on wafers for the irregular, low-area layers (periphery cuts, fuse/redundancy personalization, product variants) while periodic array layers use cheap patterning.
why: Mask cost and EUV dependence: removes $10M+ mask sets per product spin and EUV for irregular layers; product variants in days.

title: Bit-forward securities pre-sell future DRAM to finance fabs
idea: Po: the fab is paid for with memory not yet made. Issue tradable forward contracts on standardized gigabit deliveries 3-5 years out, bought by hyperscalers, OEMs and funds, financing ~50% of capex before groundbreaking and settling physically or against a price index.
why: Capital intensity and cyclicality: moves capex risk to buyers who need supply, lowers cost of capital ~3-5 points and breaks boom-bust underinvestment.

title: Photoresist that stays: patternable oxide becomes the device layer
idea: Po: the resist is the product. Use hafnium/zirconium oxo-cluster photoresists that, after exposure and anneal, densify into HfZrO dielectric or hard mask left in place, eliminating the deposit-coat-expose-etch-strip chain for those layers.
why: Process steps and tool count: ~3-4 fewer steps per affected layer, ~5-10% shorter cycle and fewer etch tools.

title: Vacuum-free spatial ALD heads for capacitor dielectrics
idea: Po: the fab runs at room pressure. Replace vacuum ALD chambers with atmospheric spatial ALD: wafers rotate under gas-bearing heads with alternating precursor zones, depositing ZrO2/HfO2 and TiN ~10x faster with no load locks or pumps.
why: Tool cost and throughput in the capacitor module: ~3-5x lower cost per wafer pass and lower energy.

title: Alignment-free capacitor carpet: cells harvest random nanorod capacitors
idea: Po: the capacitor ignores the transistor. Make a dense random carpet of isolated vertical nanorod capacitors (diameter smaller than the gap between storage-node pads) in an insulating matrix laid over the transistor array; each landing pad simply collects whatever rods sit on it, so no capacitor litho or overlay is needed.
why: Capacitor litho/overlay (facts 1,4): removes the capacitor-hole patterning layer; summing ~10-50 rods per cell tightens the Cs distribution.

title: Edge-face interconnect stacking instead of through-silicon vias
idea: Po: the wiring goes around, not through. Stack thinned DRAM dies, polish one side of the stack, route every die's I/O to that side face, and lithograph a redistribution layer there that hybrid-bonds to a logic die standing perpendicular to the stack.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): removes TSV keep-out area and TSV-yield loss, recovering ~10-20% area per bit and much of the 20-30% stack yield loss.

title: One accelerator-driven EUV light source feeds a dozen scanners
idea: Po: the scanner has no light of its own. A free-electron laser producing ~10 kW at 13.5 nm distributes light by beamlines to 10-20 scanner bodies, replacing a tin-droplet plasma source in every tool.
why: EUV cost and power: source is a big share of scanner cost and nearly all its energy; ~2-3x lower cost per EUV layer and far less power per wafer.

title: Wet crystal-plane etch carves vertical trenches in (110) silicon
idea: Po: the crystal is the mask. On (110) wafers, align line-type array features to <112> so KOH/TMAH etching stops on vertical {111} planes, giving atomically smooth slits with AR >200:1 in a wet bench for trench capacitors or line-type 3D DRAM slits.
why: Etch capex and capacitor AR (fact 1): extreme aspect ratio at near-zero tool cost, no bowing.

title: Universal half-finished wafers finished regionally as DDR, LPDDR or HBM
idea: Po: memory is finished at the customer's door. Freeze a common front end through the capacitor module, bank those wafers, and let regional back-end lines apply product-specific metal, TSV and test, so supply swings between DDR, LPDDR and HBM in weeks instead of quarters.
why: Capital efficiency: less capacity mismatch and inventory write-down, ~5-10% more usable bits from the same capex.

title: Fab in reverse: harvest DRAM dies from retired servers
idea: Po: the fab runs backwards. Industrialize de-population of retired server DIMMs and boards: desolder packages, re-ball, test and rebin them into CXL memory expanders for tier-2 workloads, with a controller that tolerates mixed speed grades.
why: Capital intensity: ~1/100 of new-fab capex per GB; hyperscalers retire tens of petabytes per year, a few percent of global bit supply available within months.

title: Fab in a tube: continuous vacuum track for capacitor module
idea: Po: the wafer never leaves the tool. Chain all ~40 capacitor-module steps (mold deposition, etch, clean, ALD, anneal) in a linear vacuum-linked track with single-wafer flow: no FOUPs, no queues, no air exposure between steps.
why: Cycle time and footprint: capacitor module from weeks to ~1 day, ~30% less WIP and floor area, fewer native-oxide cleans.

title: Memory by the square meter in idle display-panel fabs
idea: Po: RAM is made in TV factories. Idle Gen-6/8.5 LCD/OLED backplane lines already run IGZO transistors; pattern 2T0C oxide gain-cell arrays at ~1-1.5 um rules on glass (a ~5.5 m2 Gen-8.5 panel holds on the order of 20 GB), dice into tiles and bond them to 28 nm controller dies.
why: Capital intensity and non-EUV supply: zero new fab, no EUV, no quartz crucibles; ~$10-20/GB slower capacity tier from idle capacity, with IGZO's low leakage cutting refresh.

title: Depreciation arbitrage: keep paid-off 1y/1z DRAM lines running
idea: Po: the oldest fab makes the cheapest bit. Instead of converting fully depreciated 1y/1z-class DRAM lines to HBM, sign 5-year take-or-pay contracts for DDR4/LPDDR4/DDR5 at cash cost, steering auto, PC and edge demand there and freeing leading lines for AI.
why: Depreciation ~55% of wafer cost (fact 4): paid-off lines run ~40-50% cheaper per wafer, offsetting ~1.5x lower density for near-parity cost per bit at zero capex.

title: Periphery outsourced to idle 28 nm logic wafers, bonded under array
idea: Po: half the chip is missing. Existing DRAM fabs make array-only wafers (cells, bitlines, minimal local sense) while idle 28-40 nm logic fabs make periphery wafers (decoders, sense amps, I/O); the two are hybrid-bonded wafer-to-wafer with periphery under the array.
why: Periphery ~49% of die (fact 7): ~1.6-1.9x more bits per existing DRAM wafer start using surplus mature logic capacity; no new fab.

title: Self-aligned octuple patterning lets old 193i scanners print 1x-nm
idea: Po: the old scanner prints finer than its spec. Add three generations of spacer cascades (SAOP) to a 2x-nm DRAM line's existing 193i scanners so an 80 nm litho pitch becomes 10 nm lines for wordlines/bitlines; only extra ALD and etch chambers go into the existing building.
why: EUV dependence and capital: lifts an old fab ~1.5-2 nodes in density without EUV for ~10% of new-fab cost.

title: Optical-disc mastering machines write imprint templates for old fabs
idea: Po: memory is mastered like Blu-ray discs. Repurpose idle optical-disc mastering machines (rotary phase-transition thermal lithography with sub-100 nm marks) to write large-area line/dot imprint templates, which feed nanoimprint tools placed in existing 2x-nm DRAM bays for array layers.
why: Template supply and EUV avoidance: template writing at ~1% of e-beam cost on idle equipment; NIL gives sub-20 nm periodic features in trailing fabs.

title: Hard-drive head fabs make magnetic working memory
idea: Po: the disk-drive factory makes RAM. HDD read-head fabs already deposit and ion-mill sub-20 nm MTJ stacks at volume; as head demand flattens, use their deposition and milling lines to add SOT-MRAM layers onto 28 nm CMOS wafers shipped in from mature foundries, as a refresh-free DRAM-class tier.
why: Capital and U.S. manufacturability: reuses existing MTJ capacity and skills instead of building MRAM fabs; no refresh, unlimited-class endurance with SOT.

title: Image-sensor wafer-bond lines put capacitors on the backside
idea: Po: the wafer has two front sides. Use existing backside-illuminated image-sensor lines (wafer bonding, thinning to a few microns, backside litho) to flip a 40-65 nm transistor array and build tall capacitors on the freed backside, contacting drains through the thinned silicon so bitlines and capacitors stop competing for one side.
why: Capacitor wall and cell area (facts 1,7): front carries bitlines and periphery, back carries capacitors; near-4F2 layouts in trailing fabs with existing CIS tools.

title: Retired 3D NAND lines prototype 3D DRAM via replacement-gate recess
idea: Po: a NAND fab is a DRAM fab. Older 64/96-layer 3D NAND lines already run oxide/nitride stacks, high-AR hole etch, lateral nitride recess and metal fill; reuse that replacement-gate recess to carve lateral capacitor cavities and channel slots for horizontal-cell 3D DRAM, filling with Mo instead of W.
why: No manufacturable 3D DRAM yet (fact 2): paid-off tools already proven beyond 26 tiers; no new fab and less tungsten.

title: Partially-good dies become full modules through controller remap
idea: Po: the bad dies are good. Stop scrapping DRAM dies with dead banks or exhausted redundancy; bin them by usable fraction, pair 75%-good dies per slot and let a CXL or module controller remap addresses around dead regions.
why: Yield and capital: recovers ~3-8% of wafer output now scrapped, including HBM stack fallout (fact 6), with zero new fab.

title: Whole-wafer memory from an old DRAM line, never diced
idea: Po: the chip is the wafer. Run a 2x-nm DRAM flow with reticle stitching and per-reticle redundancy, keep the 300 mm wafer whole (~0.5-1 TB of bits), and bond it face-to-face to a wafer of compute or switch chiplets, skipping dicing, packaging and per-die test.
why: Packaging/test and data movement (fact 5): removes ~15-25% of cost in packaging and test; wafer-level links <1 pJ/bit; uses a depreciated fab.

title: Two bits per cell in trailing fabs with fat capacitors
idea: Po: one cell remembers two things. Old 2x-3x nm DRAM lines have larger capacitors and tighter leakage tails; store four charge levels per cell and read with reference-cell-calibrated time-to-digital sense amps (built in bonded 28 nm periphery), doubling bits on existing lines.
why: Density on existing capacity: ~1.8x bits per wafer of an old line, closing much of its gap to 1b nodes without new tools.

title: Refurbished tools fill empty shells of existing fab sites
idea: Po: factories build factories. Buy decommissioned 193i scanners, etchers and ALD tools from closing 200/300 mm lines, refurbish them and install them into unused cleanroom shell space already built at existing DRAM and logic sites.
why: Capital and time: shell and utilities (~30% of fab cost, 2+ years) are already sunk; trailing capacity online in ~12 months at ~25-35% of greenfield cost.

title: Strategic memory reserve buys gluts, contracts legacy U.S. lines
idea: Po: the government buys RAM like oil. A U.S. strategic DRAM reserve buys bits in price troughs and releases them in shortages, paired with long-term offtake contracts at existing domestic legacy DRAM lines (auto/industrial parts), smoothing the cycle that deters investment.
why: U.S. manufacturability and cyclic underinvestment: steady demand for domestic mature capacity; damps 4x price spikes.

title: Revive defunct DRAM makers' process IP in idle 300 mm lines
idea: Po: dead companies make memory. License documented flows from defunct DRAM makers (e.g., buried-wordline 4x-nm processes) and transplant them into idle U.S. 300 mm logic/foundry lines whose 193i, ALD and CMP tools already exist, producing mature DDR4/LPDDR4 parts.
why: U.S. manufacturability and time: skips ~5 years of process development; output in 2-3 years at a fraction of greenfield capex.

title: Open DRAM PDK portable across any 28-65 nm foundry
idea: Po: DRAM is open source. Publish an open, foundry-portable gain-cell/1T1C memory process design kit using only steps every 28-65 nm logic fab already runs (MIM capacitors, standard high-k, existing implants), so dozens of mature fabs can fill idle capacity with interchangeable memory dies.
why: Supply concentration and idle capacity: converts surplus mature wafer starts into multi-source memory with zero new fab.

title: Cross-company tool-hour exchange routes DRAM steps to idle tools
idea: Po: one fab has two owners. A secure scheduling exchange lets DRAM makers route non-critical steps (implant, CMP, anneal, ALD) to idle, contamination-qualified tools in nearby mature logic fabs via sealed-pod transfer, trading tool-hours like electricity.
why: Capital utilization: mature fabs often run ~70-80% utilized; borrowing hours relieves DRAM bottleneck tools ~10-15% without buying tools.

title: Modules test and burn themselves in during shipping
idea: Po: the test floor is the delivery truck. Each module gets an on-board BIST controller plus small heater and supercapacitor so burn-in, march tests and retention profiling run in transit and at first boot, reporting back to the vendor; final tester insertions shrink to a quick screen.
why: Backend capital: testers and burn-in ovens are a major backend capex and capacity bottleneck; ~50% fewer tester hours per GB.

title: Angled ion beams stretch features, deleting cut masks
idea: Po: the etcher does the lithography. Add tilted, directional ion-beam pattern-shaping chambers to existing etch bays so one exposure's holes are elongated or trimmed in a chosen direction, merging contacts or cutting lines without a second litho-etch pass.
why: Mask count and litho time in trailing fabs: removes ~1 litho-etch pair on 3-5 layers, ~10% fewer process steps.

title: Reusable seed wafers via porous-silicon layer lift-off
idea: Po: the ingot needs no crucible. Grow device-grade epitaxial silicon on a porous-silicon release layer over a reusable seed wafer in existing epi reactors, bond the device layer to a cheap carrier and lift off, reusing the seed 10-20 times.
why: Scarce resource (Spruce Pine quartz >80%): cuts Czochralski wafer demand ~5-10x per wafer start using existing epi capacity.

title: Three-mask crosspoint capacitor arrays stacked in 28 nm BEOL
idea: Po: memory with only three masks. Build stacked tiers of 1-selector-1-capacitor crosspoint cells (threshold-switch selector plus thin-film capacitor at each line crossing) in a mature foundry's BEOL with two line masks and one via mask per tier.
why: Mask count and density in trailing fabs: 4F2 per tier at F=40 nm, ~8 tiers to approach leading-node density; risk is selector off-leakage forcing ms-scale refresh.

title: Tungsten-free retrofit: molybdenum precursors in existing CVD chambers
idea: Po: memory needs no tungsten. Swap WF6 for MoO2Cl2/MoCl5 precursors in existing W CVD/ALD chambers (minor heater and delivery changes) for buried wordlines, contacts and plugs, gaining lower resistance in narrow lines.
why: Scarce resource (China ~80% of tungsten): removes W dependence with tool retrofits, no new fab; lower wordline RC as a bonus.

title: Helium-free fab: closed-loop chuck gas recapture and substitutes
idea: Po: the fab breathes no helium. Retrofit existing etch/CVD electrostatic chucks with closed-loop backside-gas recirculation and membrane purification, substitute H2/Ar or N2 where heat-transfer margin allows, and recover He from leak-check and stage purges.
why: Helium chokepoint (Qatar ~30% offline): cuts fab helium purchases ~80-90%, protecting output of existing lines.

title: Inductive coil links stack trailing DRAM dies without TSVs
idea: Po: the stack is wireless. Stack thinned DRAM dies from existing lines and pass data vertically through near-field inductive coils drawn in standard top metal (no TSV etch, fill or reveal), with power delivered by edge wire bonds or a few large vias.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): removes the TSV module and much of its area/yield tax, enabling HBM-like stacks from trailing fabs at ~1 pJ/bit.
